subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words on the budget that was introduced last Thursday. I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) with great interest, and I do not rise to speak in this debate as a financial expert, but as an individual who wants to express his opinion on a budget that the Minister of Finance has tried to defend and about which he has tried to arouse enthusiasm.
Mr. Speaker, I read this budget many times on my way to my constituency for the weekend. I would have liked to prepare these remarks better, but I did not have time to do so, because my train was late today.
I am always astonished when I compare Canada's budget with that of other countries with almost the same population. This country, with a $13 billion budget for 20 million citizens, does not succeed in providing the necessaries of life to low-income families and in solving once and for all the situation with regard to consumption.
We do wonder, Mr. Speaker, and like all the others, we try to find where the problem lies. I, for one, maintain that we overspend on administration and underspend on participation. Very little money is paid out to those who stand in need of it.
For instance, the Department of Agriculture estimates total several hundred millions of dollars, but if we take the administration costs into consideration, we are utterly astonished to realize how little farmers get. That is why I said earlier that too much money goes into administration and none is left for those who would need it so much.
This budget once again reflects the erroneous mentality of bureaucracy. The minister contends that the expansionary fiscal and monetary measures he took are beginning to show results which will further improve. He said that most economic indicators show an improvement of the Canadian economy and that unemployment is easing off. This one is a bit steep and if the minister would take a tour around my region, he would notice immediately that unemployment is not easing off at all.
The first measure proposed by the minister is designed to jack up unemployment benefits. Indeed, I would like to make a few remarks on this point.
While benefits were expected, according to the rumours from the government side, to be doubled, they will be raised by 10 per cent only, and this is not likely to solve the unemployment problem in the least. The sufferings of the unemployed will continue.


December 7, 1970

In my region, the problem is not one of whether the benefits are going to be raised or not. The minister should have thought of changing the unemployment insurance regulations by requiring, for instance, a smaller number of stamps. To qualify for benefits, a worker needs 30 stamps but he can never work long enough to accumulate that many unemployment insurance stamps.
In my constituency, hundreds of workers are not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits because they have not accumulated enough stamps. After two, three, four of five weeks of discussion, they are told that this is a regrettable situation, but they will have to seek help elsewhere.
This is when they are directed to welfare offices. For a family of five, six or seven children, welfare is no fun. However welfare allowances are expected to double in my region since the workers have been unable to accumulate stamps and are not entitled to allowances.
If the minister or his officials had made the effort to further study the allowance increase so as to permit the unemployed to cope with a higher cost of living, they would thus have solved the most urgent problem. In addition, the minister told us that loans in the amount of $150 million will be granted to the provinces through a fund intended to stimulate the economy and this money will be used to finance, during the year to come, job-creating investment projects.
Mr. Speaker, there again loans are involved. The government merely says: We are ready to support the provinces, the municipalities and the companies wishing to borrow, so that they can get deeper into debt.
We have only two money sources, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) says, taxing and borrowing. And these estimates point to borrowing.
On this matter of borrowing, I read a newspaper article reporting what the Quebec Premier thinks of the benefits offered the provinces by the government. I believe that he was expecting something other than availability of loans. I quote:
For the first time in several years, the Quebec Minister of Finance can indulge in the luxury of choice between several options: borrow slightly less than last year on the money markets or improve Quebec's credit rating; or maintain borrowing at its present level and use surplus liquidity to convert into debenture loan part of the short-term commitments of the government toward school boards, for instance; or borrow more this year and increase capital expenditures and several extrabudgetary items such as government investments in SOF and Soquem.
As concerns the cyclical stabilization fund dealt with by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), here is what I read in a newspaper:
It is therefore quite a service that Edgar Benson has rendered his Quebec colleague. Nevertheless, it should be mentioned that the new $150 million fund is not yet exactly the contingency assistance fund called for last June by the premier of Quebec.
Mr. Bourassa had proposed the establishment of permanent machinery; the program announced by Mr. Benson will terminate in a year and a half. Mr. Bourassa wanted the contingency assistance fund to be replenished by statute with certain federal taxes, which would vary according to the needs; the funds made
23568-44$
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
available to the provinces will come from the consolidated revenue of the central government and their importance is left entirely to the discretion of the latter. Mr. Bourassa had suggested that the contingency assistance fund give the provinces both loans and grants; the federal Minister of Finance has kept only the loans.
That is what we regret. Had the Minister of Finance followed all the suggestions of the present premier of Quebec, we would not have to deal only with loans, borrowing and mortgages in connection with the provinces. It must not be forgotten that the sum of $150 million will be used in so far as the province of Quebec is able to borrow and municipalities and other organizations keep on running into debt.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I wonder where we will end up with all those debts, and whether we are not doing the provinces a disservice by allowing them to double their debt without ever getting direct help that does not lead to debt.
But, what can be done? Our present financial system is made for debts, and must make the best of it. After collecting about $13 billion in taxes from the people, the federal government asks the provinces to go into debt for it. The minister proposes as a third measure, and I quote:
-it is intended to allocate a further sum of $23 milion to departments and agencies to undertake further capital improvements in regions where unemployment is most severe.
When considering that $23 million are divided among the various departments, I immediately think of the Department of Agriculture. Indeed, I am anxious to see what will be the amount allotted to that department especially in Quebec, because the budget does not propose any measure to promote agriculture in that province. I trust that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) will take into account the different letters he receives and that he will take the necessary steps, in order to stimulate Quebec agriculture.
I am anxious to see what steps will be taken, because I would like some of those credits to be affected to farming in my area where 75 per cent of the people are connected with farming and need some help comparable with that received in other areas. Our district has experienced some disasters and I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will let us know the amount that the Minister of Finance wants to give the department of Agriculture and the sum that will be forthcoming for our regions.
The minister also stated as follows:
A further $20 million will be allocated to development of roads.
It is no use hoping to get any thing for our regions. It is for Montreal. This sum of $20 million will be spent on the development of the new airport and will not alleviate in any way unemployment in our region.
As the minister stated, the purpose of this budget is to stimulate the Canadian economy and alleviate unemployment. Of course, the big problem today is unemployment. But what causes this unemployment? First of all, the

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Gauthier
increase in interest rates has favoured the big fellow to the detriment of the little one.
Today measures are proposed to reduce unemployment when for two years there was harping on inflation. Inflation has never existed at the level of the worker, of the small wage earner, but rather at the level of big finance. The government is still promoting the latter to create inflation.
The government is presenting both ineffectual and temporary measures to give assistance to the low-wage earner and the unemployed. Such measures will have no immediate effect in my area.
As for the $40 million for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, once again is a measure which, because of the high rate of interest and the very strict terms imposed by that agency, will have no effect. No family man with an average income can build a home in my district. That is the situation for all those who wish to build a low-cost home. I know that the loans are far the big contractors and not for the average citizen.
In my region there is a housing shortage. The $40 million will be used for building about 4,000 homes. In my opinion, this is not a solution for the family man who needs a dwelling and must pay a very high rent because he has many children. In cities nowadays landlords refuse to rent to a family with five children.
The government will have to find a better formula. If it does not want to lower interest rates for fear of antagonizing financiers, let it give at least rebate to average wage earners so that they may build a house.
In this budget speech, the minister also said that:
The proposals set out in the White Paper on Income Security will have important fiscal and economic implications which will mean additional payments of $200 million and a new redistribution of income for those in the lower income group and the less favoured areas.
We agree with the principle of old age pensions, but not to give the older people a guaranteed income, as is proposed; this is only a pretext to appoint hundreds of inspectors merely to go and search senior citizens' homes to see if they have hidden $50 or $100.
[DOT] (5:10 pun.)
That is why we are calling for across-the-board allowances and pensions, to avoid the expense of 3,000 inspectors snooping in homes to check on whether a certain senior citizen is not getting $5 or $10 more than he should. In fact, I believe the guaranteed income costs as much in inspections and salaries as the senior citizen is getting.
If we give old people a flat-rate pension, those who do not need it should reimburse it when making out their income tax returns. The Taxation Division is well enough organized to make the relevant inquiries, which would do away with the two inspection systems we now have.
Every week-end, we are faced with 30 or 40 cases of old people being dealt with unfairly. The inquiry was not carried out properly and we have to go back and find the error. We manage to do it but at the cost of God knows how many headaches. The government should pay out pensions whenever practicable and put an end to its policy of distributing grants only to create employment.
Let us do away with administrative costs and inspectors' salaries, and then we will be in a position to hand out to our older citizens increased pensions without increased taxation.
The same is liable to happen with respect to family allowances. A system set up to investigate to the last cent expended is also recommended in this instance. There is going to be a reduction in the amount of family allowances paid to the wife of a man earning $4,500 or more.
Never will $16 be granted for each child, except to a few families but the rest will need it too. In fact, the head of a family who earns $6,000 or $7,000 a year but who has 7, 8 or 9 children will not be so much better off.
I have here an article published in today's newspaper and signed by Mr. Paul Sauriol, about family allowances. He is presently in favour of this measure, of course, because all the press as well as Information Canada, which is financed by the government and speaks up for its policies, would be hard put to it to give an unbiased opinion. However, this is what Paul Sauriol writes:
The proposed change in family allowances is the only one of the three where the government really advocates dropping universal benefits in favour of selective allowances.
The monthly allowances would be increased to $16 per child for families with an income of $4,500 or less, and the allowances would be gradually reduced as the family income increases and they would cease completely for families with an income in excess of $10,000 a year.
When the head of a family earns $10,000 a year but has 11 children he cannot be said to be rich. And in relation to that I quote further:
One thing must be said, first of all: the real value of family allowances, their purchasing power, has greatly diminished these last few years as a result of price increases, so that the $16 per child given to underprivileged families would merely reestablish the former purchasing power of present allowances.
The principle of selective assistance to most disadvantaged families is excellent, but the decreasing rate suggested in the white paper has one serious defect, because it does not take into consideration the number of children in a family, nor their age. Wednesday's papers mentioned the case of one family where the father earns a little more than $10,000 and where the twelve children are eligible for allowances. Under the proposed reform, that family would not be entitled to any allowance while another one with three children and having an income of $7,000 would get $33 per month. The family-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really had hoped to deal at some length with the intelligent contributions made to

December 7, 1970

the debate by speakers for the opposition, but unfortunately so far I have been unable to find anything sufficiently constructive to really counter. As a matter of fact, they discounted themselves by the weaknesses of their arguments and by the contradictions which were prevalent. However, I suppose that is to be expected because they have their job to do and they have to extend themselves to face a budget as strong as this is. But now that the big guns are coming up in the debate-I understand I am to be followed by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees)-I think the tempo should pick up and excitement reign as this House deserves.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I feel, in all sincerity, that this was a most imaginative budget because it dealt with the issues as they are and not as we would like them to be, and it dealt with them in a realistic manner. We were able to look at things in specific terms and in the total context of the situation that faces our country as a great trading nation in the world today, bearing in mind the program we have had for the last many months to curb inflation which has had a high degree of success, with the unfortunate side effects that were regrettably to be expected and certainly greater than we had wished.
We have used very specific and sharp instruments rather than the broader, blunt instruments which the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) suggested. The opposition always have neat packages, but today they had a great, big package of actions which they advocated with no real understanding of the consequences of those actions. I am not saying they advocated the wrong action, but it is not the one we chose. We chose to deal with the problems in our country that are of a regional nature to a large extent, and we are trying to zero in on them.
I think that the budget policies have been particularly consistent and they are part of an over-all program. I do not think the Budget can be isolated from other programs which this government is undertaking. It should be considered in relation to the white paper on tax reform, that on income security and that on unemployment insurance, plus the fiscal and monetary policies of the government as well as the actions of the Prices and Income Commission. I think these things express the philosophy of the government and are the articulated steps to deal with our problems.
What is most important in the budget is a rejection of the old, standard, universal type of program which was perhaps good in its times. Perhaps as a result of welfare programs and policies of this type, which we followed over the past years, our economy has changed and has shifted. Today when we talk of a middle income group, we really mean the group in the $10,000 to $25,000 income range. I think it is a fortunate country that has a middle income group with that size of income, but that is not the fact, we have replaced the principle of universality with an attach on specific problems.
The Budget-Mr. Danson
I think the government was well intentioned, and certainly it was an opportune time to try to eliminate a means which is demean ng. It is something which we would not like to face and we would not like to see other people face, nor is it generally administratively efficient. The result, however, was that those who really needed help in our expanding and affluent society were getting less help, and those who did not need it were getting it. This was costly and inefficient. Now, we are zeroing in on those people who need help. I do not suggest for a moment that we are doing as much as is necessary or as much as we would wish. I think we are doing as much as we can, and we are doing it in stages.
There is a minimum of pump priming. The things that are being presented in this budget and in our other programs are those which are economically viable, and this is extremely important. There is not much point in pouring money down the drain in welfare programs. Some must be continued, but to the extent possible we should build the type of programs that help sustain themselves and help to lift up the deprived so that they can be self sustaining. There are those who suggest that by providing this type of assistance to people we are creating a welfare society, a type of society that depends on welfare, people who are permanently on welfare. That has been the case to a large extent in the past, but we are trying to overcome this tendency to have generations in the same family develop a welfare psychology.
Certainly, these people are the exception rather than the rule. As I understand it from surveys that have been done both in this country and elsewhere, a very high percentage of those people in receipt of welfare are unemployable for a large number of reasons. Some 45 per cent are unemployable because of physical or mental disability. They just cannot work or they are too old. Well over one third are women who have been abandoned, who are divorced or widowed and are left with dependent children still of school age. When you distil this down, less than 5 per cent of welfare recipients are able to work but are not working. Sociologists tell us that even among this group, there are undetected psychological problems which might prevent them from working These studies were carried out in Canada and also in the United States. The results in both countries were amazingly close. It would be a shame to think that this group of less than 5 per cent is typical.
There are those who advocate throwing out welfare programs because there are those who abuse them But there is no point in throwing out the baby with the'bath water, and I suggest that all those who abuse our government programs and our tax systems are not welfare recipients. There are many people who are quite affluent and who abuse our system in one way or another, so let us not pick on that small group.
I think we realize that equalization payments, which are part of our system and have been good in the past have not been adequate to deal with the disparities in our regions. Those of us who come from favoured

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Danson
areas-and I consider the area from which I come as being particularly favoured-are conscious of the fact that we are favoured because we are part of Canada and only in a united and prosperous Canada can we remain favoured. However, we hope we will all be equally favoured. If the other parts of the country are able to become economically viable so that unemployment is decreased and people are prosperous, then we from the Toronto region for instance would benefit from that because they are our markets and we become theirs. The trade and prosperity that is generated helps to lift up all of us. In this respect, and particularly in view of recent events, I think those of us from such favoured regions are happy to see our government take an initiative to help pull other parts of the country closer to the level which we enjoy.
Perhaps we are disappointed in some ways that we will not have a tax reduction, but I suggest we might have had a tax increase as a result of these programs because these programs will make us more prosperous and the more money we make, the more taxes we pay. I do not object to taxes of that sort. But by the same token, even though we come from a favoured region, the urgency of other programs is no reason for neglecting the legitimate needs of the great urban centres which are prosperous also. I refer to the expansion of airport facilities in Toronto and the many other factors that necessarily have to be dealt with in a growing urban area.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Information Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Information Canada could tell us a great deal, and I am sure it will.
The interesting part of the programs in the budget is the recognition that society has changed, that government has changed, and that the relationship of one to the other has changed considerably. In years gone by, in the days when government expenditures were something like 7 per cent of the gross national product, the government played a small part in our lives. But today, when you consider all the levels of government, we are talking in terms of 40 or 45 per cent of the gross national product which passed through the hands of government. Government is a big factor in our lives. It would be nice to say that less government is the best government, but that is not the case. First, it is not necessarily the best-I am not suggesting it could not be better-but less government is not going to be the case in our time. I think any realistic person who examines what is happening now will realize that government has improved. What we have done is blend the private and public sectors, and it is important that we continue to do this. The government should act as a conduit to the public sector, directing the economy to the extent that is necessary, and no more, so that we can all prosper by it.
e (5:30 p.m.)
In the budget speech on December 3, at page 1741 of Hansard the minister referred to provision of a further $40 million to the capital budget of Central Mortgage and

Housing. In August $100 million was added, and some $200 million has been provided for low-cost housing. This stresses the direction the government is taking. The government has infused in the order of $1 billion into the private sector and the construction industry primarily for low-cost housing. This is where the help is needed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is needed this winter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is where help is needed, rather than for high-cost housing. The money will start the program moving. We have signalled our intention to help the economy in this way, and I think this is important. The hon. member for Waterloo spoke at some length about the provisions for accelerated depreciation and gave all the reasons why he thought this was bad. This is not to be done all at once, but at least we are telling the economy that we are starting to expand in this direction. We must be careful, however, not to overdo this because of the success we have had so far with our anti-inflation programs.
If the hon. member for Waterloo wants to list the reasons why accelerated depreciation is bad, he may do so; but I would like to quote from a memo which an eminent economist wrote to himself on October 20. This was B. J. Danson, M.P., outlining why he felt accelerated depreciation is good. Occasionally, when I have thoughts I try to put them in writing in order to develop some degree of logic. Therefore I said to myself that aside from the infusion of mortgage funds for housing, which we have in great measure, I believed the most effective and least costly tool could be the acceleration of depreciation on capital equipment for industry. This might follow the pattern of double depreciation used in 1962, although the degree of impetus to the economy could be controlled by the degree of acceleration. In other words, rather than the current 20 per cent on machinery it could be that 25 per cent or 33J per cent would be more adequate.
Amongst the advantages is the relatively limited effect on revenue as opposed to massive spending programs. The effect on revenue is great-$25 million in the first year and $250 million over the whole period. This is positive spending and not pump-priming spending. Then many deferred expansion programs would be freed because we know there will be incentive for this type of program. This would considerably offset some of the pessimism that has existed in the business community.
Another advantage is that jobs would be created immediately in the engineering and construction of the machinery itself, plus the concurrent auxiliary expansion necessary to house and service it. When new machinery is delivered, the utilization of it creates more jobs. The hon. member for Waterloo suggested that it eliminates jobs because of increased efficiency. Certainly this might be a factor, but I would hate to see our economy sponsor increased inefficiency in order to create jobs or continued inefficiency. Productivity would increase by means of additional modem capacity and the replacement of older and less efficient equipment.

December 7, 1970
Smaller companies, frequently Canadian-owned with limited resources, would be encouraged more readily than larger corporations whose decisions are less influenced by limitations on available capital. This could be an area where the question of Canadian ownership could be enhanced as was suggested by an hon. member. There could be greater incentives for Canadian-owned businesses. I do not think that this is an area where we want to build up nationalism, but we do want to give impetus to productivity and efficiency. Flexibility can be obtained through the rate at which or the period in which purchases must be made. The experience of the early sixties was highly successful and gave considerable impetus to Canadian-owned companies even though there were no qualifications regarding nationality.
Another factor which we might consider is allowing this accelerated depreciation under the regional expansion program. I understand this program does not so qualify at the present time. We would develop some flexibility in our regional expansion program through capital cost acceleration. We have already introduced the principle of using 115 per cent of value for depreciation purposes at existing rates. I should like this principle to be watched very closely in order to make sure that it does not overheat the economy. By the same token, the areas of greatest industrial concentration naturally have the greatest potential for unemployment of skilled workers, and this is happening already. I submit that this provision in the budget will help alleviate that condition.
A matter which may be related to the budget, and one which was raised at the hearings on tax reform-I believe it is mentioned also in the report on the status of women-is aid to day care centres. This question was not included in the report of the finance committee, but a submission was made in the brief by the Vanier Institute for the Family to the effect that day care centres should be encouraged. I think this could be achieved by a budgetary measure.
It is good business to have more women in the work force, and the provision of day care facilities would encourage them to return to work. I do not believe that most businessmen have thought seriously of this, however. If we consider providing something like a 150 per cent write-off for the expense in the first year of establishing day care facilities, we might find them more interested. It makes good business sense and good social sense. Women would be happy to work, knowing that their children would be taken care of and it would be a great contribution to the morale and efficiency of our society.
Another area for concern is summer student employment, which will soon face us. In considering this question I have come to the conclusion that no one massive program will look after all students but, rather, what is required is a mass of programs, each one to look after some students. I was surprised and delighted at the success of the program for hiring students which was provided by our armed services last summer. It seemed to work out well for the students, and the armed services appeared to be happy with it. Having had that success, we should look at ways to improve that program rather
The Budget-Mr. Danson
than just providing more bodies for square-bashing. Perhaps the program could be developed as a paramilitary peace corps in Canada, with the students becoming involved in questions of the environment, ecology, pollu-tino clean-up and the like. In my own city of Toronto I should like to see them work on cleaning up the Don River.
I understand that Arctic command has some ideas germinating about taking students into the Arctic in the summer. They could work with the native people and help in the new communities by cleaning up the filth in the rivers and elsewhere. Perhaps this would serve to get young people enthused about the Arctic. If a few hundred were to start on such a program, some would become Arctic oriented. Some might become so Arctic oriented that they would be willing to devote their futures to it. I think that would be great for this country. In subsequent years, those who went there previously could help other students in going to the Arctic. I think the Arctic is a practical area for this kind of activity.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Last night I spoke at a function known as police appreciation night at the Centennial Baptist Church, Markham, in my constituency. It occurred to me that it might be worth while to have students during the summer months working with our police forces. It would improve their appreciation of what the police have to do and contend with. These students could talk to their fellow students about their experiences. The experience would be a revelation. Also, some of our youth might be inspired to make law enforcement their career. Our police forces at all levels ought to participate in that kind of program, which would be of minimum cost and extremely helpful. When I spoke to ex-chief Mackay of the Toronto police, who has now gone to greener pastures as chairman of the Liquor Licence Board, I learned that he thought this suggestion was worth while. Apparently it is not new. He also felt that people should be encouraged to a greater extent to employ summer students in their homes and cottages.
There are many other things I should like to talk about at this time. However, there are other members who wish to speak and I shall close my remarks by making one more point relating to national objectives. I am certainly not trying to articulate our national objectives at this time. Some of our difficulties stem from the fact that we must work from election to election. It is not that we do not try to think of the long-term; it is merely that our thinking is circumscribed by the fact that we must face an election every four years or so. Nevertheless, the Economic Council is looking at the long-range picture. The Prices and Incomes Commission seems to be looking at some of our short-range problems. These problems are always present and affect management, labour and society in general.
It seems to me that if we could bring these disparate bodies of society together we would see, if we could look far enough ahead, that all of our national objectives are identical and that the things we each want in Canada for our children or for our children's children are the

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Hees
things we want for society as a whole. If we could bring all these various groups together we would see, if we could look far enough ahead, that we have a mutuality of interest in the solution of our common problems and that we have common objectives. I think it would be found that our objectives and even our methods are not mutually exclusive. We could then fill in the gaps in greater harmony.
Since I know that we are to be favoured with an address by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), and because more members are now entering the House-they want to listen to him-and time is getting on, I shall defer to the hon. member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I start by thanking the Parliamentary Secretary for his graciousness in terminating his remarks, thereby giving me a chance to finish my speech before six o'clock. I appreciate this very much indeed.
The budget that has been presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) I believe could be summed up as an expenditure of $500 million to try to bolster the economy which, because of lack of positive government economic policies, has been allowed to run down in a rather shocking fashion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We all hope that this infusion of $500 million will greatly reduce unemployment. We can only wait to see what the results will be, hoping that they will be successful. I believe this budget pays far too little attention to incentives to stimulate the economy and make it possible for employment not to be provided just on a temporary basis as a result of construction projects but on a continuing and expanding basis. I believe that by stimulating the economy we could provide the expansion of our continuing economic processes, those processes carried out by industry, so that we could have not simply an increase in employment now but a continual increase of employment because the economy would be stimulated, would be moving faster and would be continuing to employ more and more people.
I believe that the 115 per cent capital cost allowance is a move in the right direction and will no doubt result in additional purchases of capital equipment which would not otherwise be made. I believe there are three other moves that the government could and should make at this time to stimulate the economy. First, it should bring great pressure to bear-and I know that these people listen when pressure is applied-on the chartered banks of this country to lower their commercial lending rates so that construction and the general operations of industry can be expanded and employment increased.
Second, I believe the government should introduce tax incentives in the form of tax rebates paid on the basis of increased productivity, which would induce industry to make the necessary expenditures on new plant, equipment and production systems which are needed in order
to lower costs and selling prices, thus making our products more competitive, making it possible to sell them in greater volume and thereby enabling more people to be employed.
Third, I believe the government should announce that it has decided not to cancel the 21 per cent tax on the first $35,000 of corporate profits, which tax is particularly important to small businesses. It should announce that the 21 per cent tax will remain and will not be replaced by the regular 50 per cent rate. This kind of move, Mr. Speaker, is very much needed to restore the confidence of business in the future of the economy, and to persuade industry that it is justified in making the expansionary moves which we all know are being held back in large number at the present time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is making it impossible to employ the number of people we should like to see employed in our country.
I should like to speak for a few moments on the position of the Auditor General, who has been brought under attack very severely by this government during the past few weeks. Actually, there has been by the government a process of attack on the Auditor General for the past several years. These attacks have been brought to a head rather spectacularly during the past few weeks. For many years, as we know, this country has benefited greatly by having the expenditures of the federal government checked and commented upon in the yearly review to Parliament known as the Auditor General's report. Although the primary job of the Auditor General is to see that proper accounts are kept by all government departments, he is also authorized by the legislation to report on any matter that he considers should be brought to the attention of the House of Commons.
All governments, both past and present, have been embarrassed from time to time by disclosures of wasteful spending of public funds. This has made them more careful about expenditures in the future and the country has benefited as a consequence. From time to time, Mr. Speaker, when I was a minister I was shocked to learn from the Auditor General's report of stupid mistakes which departments for which I was responsible had made. Although it was extremely embarrassing at the time, the knowledge that a watchdog had a constant eye on our operations made me and those who worked for me do a better job of running the departments for which we were responsible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

All the members of the government did a better job because of the careful and constant watch which the Auditor General kept on all moneys spent by departments. But, Mr. Speaker, by the presentation of

December 7, 1970

the government's bill in respect of the Auditor General, all this was to be changed. The proposed bill would have taken away the right which the Auditor General enjoys under the legislation.

The hon. member knows one does not reflect in this House upon decisions of the House. The bill has been withdrawn; we cannot go back to it and discuss it in this debate. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I ask Your Honour to note that the interjection of the hon. member has taken approximately four minutes of my time. I would appreciate it if I could go to four minutes past six o'clock in order to complete my remarks. As I said before I was so rudely interrupted, the proposed bill would have taken away the right which the Auditor General enjoys under the present legislation of calling to the attention of Parliament instances of wasteful spending of public funds that have come to his attention. I refer to such items as the Bonaventure, the $8 million St. Lawrence harbour that will never be used, and the approaches to the Prince Edward Island causeway. The proposed bill would have restricted him essentially to a bookkeeping function with no right to comment on bureaucratic mistakes and extravagances.
Hon. members know that the first move along the road to dictatorship is the removal of criticism by a government or would-be dictator. That the government would think it could get away with a move which would have
The Budget-Mr. Hees
removed it from detailed and informed criticism for misuse of funds is a shocking example of arrogance and is a measure of how far this government has moved along the road to dictatorship.
This measure was obviously aimed at the present Auditor General, Maxwell Henderson. Over the years, under both Liberal and Conservative governments Mr. Henderson has been diligent in reporting to Parliament and the public instances of wasteful and foolish government spending. This has apparently irritated cabinet ministers and senior civil servants to the point where today they have decided that at all costs and in any way available to them he will be removed from office. If they had succeeded it would have been one of the most serious blows ever struck at parliamentary government in this country. The time to stop this march toward dictatorship is now.
Even before last week the opposition made it very clear that they intended to fight every inch of the way this latest move to suppress criticism. As a consequence of this determination the government lost whatever courage it posessed, which was very little, turned tail and ran. However, Mr. Speaker, the government's position has been made very clear by the undermining of the position of the Auditor General-which members of the cabinet have systematically undertaken, by the downgrading of his staff and the undisguised hostility which members of the cabinet openly show toward him.
The position of the Auditor General should be further protected from this government and any future power-hungry government which would like to prevent any criticism of its actions. I am convinced that further protection should be given to the Auditor General by requiring a two-thirds vote of both Houses of Parliament in order to remove him from office, instead of the present simple majority. A simple majority vote enables a government with an over-all majority, such as the present Liberal government which also has a majority in the Senate, simply to call in its members and vote him out of office.
The hostile attitude of the government makes it obvious that added protection is needed for the office if the Auditor General is to continue to carry out the very valuable task which he performs for the people of Canada. I believe that such a move should be brought before Parliament at the earliest possible moment, for the benefit of parliamentary government in this country.
