subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on the budget statement he delivered to this House last week. I believe Canadians should hear more statements of this type. In addition, his address contained a budget which I believe will strike with pinpoint accuracy at the most troublesome areas of unemployment in the country.
However, it is not so much the budget itself I wish to discuss tonight as the statement which went with it and the confidence displayed in that statement, though the budget itself was certainly well thought-out and contained a program vastly better than anything presented in the last few hours by spokesmen for the opposition parties. But let us consider the budget statement for a few minutes and examine some of the confident statements which the minister made, together with some of the facts to which he drew our attention as far as the Canadian economy is concerned.
My hon. friend pointed out that employment is, in fact, rising in Canada and that unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis appears to be decreasing. He went on to say that real output in the economy is rising. Later he told the House we were experiencing a considerable boom in housing in Canada and that apart from housing, capital investment was strong. He said, further, that 1970 would go on record as the best year ever in international trade. Last, he informed us that Canada had achieved a record envied by other countries in the world in putting the brakes on price increases. From the third quarter of 1969 to the third quarter of 1970, consumer prices rose by only 3 per cent compared with 5.7 per cent in the United States and even larger increases in many other countries. Only one country had a better record, Finland, with an increase of 2.8 per cent.
The minister did not paint a completely rosy picture. He admitted there was an unemployment problem and said that the rate of growth of employment must improve. But all in all it was a very optimistic and confident statement, the kind of statement which is rarely heard in Canada these days. Sometimes, when we display optimism of this kind as we discuss the prospects of our country we are accused of being stupidly patriotic. Generally, when this House discusses the future of our country and the prospects of its economy we display a most pessimistic attitude. This negative or pessimistic attitude is evident throughout the country as it is in this House. I noticed it on the evening the Minister of Finance made his statement. Whenever he expressed confidence in the Canadian economy or in the future of this country there were snickers and guffaws from the opposition benches.
This is indicative of the attitude taken by some members of this House, including the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I have heard it expressed on other occasions; for example, during the debate on the Speech from the Throne. But it does not alter the fact that the vast majority of the people still have great confidence in

this country. I believe we have to fight the type of negative attitude displayed by some people in this country and in this House. It is nothing new. The pages of history are filled with pessimistic predictions as to Canada's future. The one which perhaps most ludicrously underestimated Canada's potential appeared in an English newspaper of 1871 as follows:
A word or two on Canadian finances in general would be in season. Canada is one of the most overrated colonies we have. The country is poor and crushed with debt. The province and city of Quebec are notoriously bankrupt.
In the end, the Dominion will have to go into liquidation. One day, when the load gets too heavy, Ontario is pretty certain to go over to the States, into which it dovetails and where its best trade outlet is.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I suggest it is time we began to develop a positive attitude in relation to the prospects for this country, which are certainly very bright indeed. The attitude of people in this country seems to be that that we should criticize everybody and everything. This includes foreign countries. It is time we began to look at the good things in Canada and to take an optimistic and positive approach, the type of approach that the Minister of Finance took in his budget.
I should like to quote from a recent article that appeared in the Banff Crag and Canyon in which the editor was berating the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for its anti-American attitude. In a constructive spirit he suggested that the CBC should present a program on what a good country Canada is and how we as citizens can make it even better. He went on to say:
Maybe a series on the opportunities to get away from it all in the north and the chances to make a good living there.
Certainly, there are plenty of people in other parts of the world who would welcome the chance to come to Canada-[DOT] to enjoy the things we take for granted.
The CBC should be pointing out, to Canadians, the many good things that await them right in their own country and forget about wasting the taxpayers' money on expensive programming beating the daylights out of the United States of America.
Those people who take a negative approach seem to think that government should do everything for them. They criticize government because it is not doing enough, and seem concerned only with what government can do for them personally. I suggest this approach is not only improper but does not display the type of positive attitude that has brought this country to its present state of prosperity, an attitude it will be necessary to adopt in the future to bring about even greater prosperity. Those who take a negative approach feel that some powerful central authority, be it a provincial or federal government, will look after them. Instead of expecting the impossible, I suggest these people should show a little initiative and attempt to improve their own position, as they could well do if only they would so determine.
Many people in this country have the idea that it is a wealthy country, that Canada has great resources, that the land is rich and that from the land and its resources we can do well economically both as a nation and as individuals. I suggest that the time when we can do this
December 7, 1970

is almost over. It is time we began to think, not of what we can get from the land to make ourselves wealthier but what we ourselves can contribute to this country.
I was interested to note that of all the industrialized nations of the world, Canada appears to be the least inventive. According to my information, residents of at least ten major countries filed patent applications at rates very much in excess of the rate in Canada. For every one patent application filed in Canada by a Canadian, 18 are filed by foreigners. Canada's rate of inventiveness is probably the lowest in the entire world. I suggest this is because we expect the country to be rich, to give everything to us. We do not use our intuition and apply our talents to the inventing and devising of methods to improve our economic situation and to develop technology. I suggest this attitude is due to our negative outlook.
I should also like to quote from an article that appeared several months ago in a leading United States daily. This article very much reflects my own opinion of the attitude of people toward government and toward what they expect from government, and illustrates how individual initiative contributes toward both economic and social growth. The article reads, in part:
There are few greater powers on earth than the cumulative
effect of individual initiative rightly directed-
Today, as they look about them, men are staggered by the immensity and the complexity of the problems confronting them. The threat of war, spreading pollution, racial bitterness, vast poverty, urban blight, crime and violence, the withering away of moral and religious standards, personal and public tensions, these and many more challenges bewilder the individual. And, to a degree unprecedented in history, millions look to some central source of public authority to save them.
But one need only talk with wise public officials, with thoughtful political scientists, with insightful historians to perceive how fruitless it is to look to such central authority to make the world, or a nation, right.
What is required is the awakening of a realization that most of these problems-above all, those which stem from a lowering of personal and civic standards-can only be solved through a massive grass roots effort. There must come the time when the average individual recognizes that he must actively participate in solving one or more of the problems which he sees around him.
Such individual effort has a breadth, a sweep, an inspiration which no organized government program can equal.
I believe that is the type of initiative that comes from taking a positive approach. It is the attitude that is engendered by the sort of positive statements that the minister made last week in his budget address which help to build a belief in Canada, a belief that will foster economic growth. Aside from the benefits that will accrue from the programs announced in the budget, the optimism and confidence expressed in the speech are a very good sign for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
nave to agree with one remark made by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Sula-tycky) namely, that the statement we heard last Thursday evening from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is the kind of statement that is not too often made. On behalf of the Canadian people I say thank God it is not made
The Budget-Mr. Carter
too often. It is quite obvious that what the colleagues of the Minister of Finance refer to as a budget speech is nothing more than the confession of the Minister of Finance and the government that their illogical and insane policies, their so-called war on inflation and their deliberate attempt to create unemployment have had, as we on this side of the House predicted, a ruinous effect on the economy of this country. This government has forced the economy to the brink of disaster by its illogical and ill-conceived policies to fight inflation.
Sitting in this chamber and watching the Minister of Finance deliver his address last Thursday night, one got the impression that his skin was so thick that in comparison a rhinoceros would be a sensitive creature. The Minister of Finance demonstrated to the Canadian public that he does not know where his economic policies are taking this country. Certainly, this budget is the latest piece of documentary evidence we have had to prove this point.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Last March we saw the minister stand in his place and say to the Canadian people that the brakes were on. The words he then used were "restraint," "cutback" and "tighten the government's purse strings." He said a surplus was essential for our economic well-being, and to hell with unemployment; because the Minister of Finance, as did his leader the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), made the statement that they were prepared to drive unemployment to an all-time high in an endeavour to win their so-called, phony war on inflation.
In his budget speech on Thursday night, without batting an eyelash the minister performed a complete about-face. Instead of forecasting a budgetary surplus of some $300 million, he said there would be a deficit of $320 million. In spite of the fact that we have a seriously sick economy with probably the highest rate of unemployment in years, with housing starts right across the country, especially in the Atlantic region, at an all-time low, with profits and volume of new business declining rapidly, the minister talked as if the economy was never better and is going ahead full blast. The minister would have us believe that the economy is advancing in leaps and bounds, that the unemployment situation is rapidly disappearing and that seasonally adjusted unemployment is rapidly falling off.
The minister would have us believe that we are having a boom in housing and that we will go into 1971 with an all-time high and, as he stated, one of our best years in international trade. It is quite obvious that the minister is being fooled by his own figures, because in 1970 the unemployment figure rose to an almost all-time high, with predictions being made by competent economists and those who are eminently qualified to make such predictions that unemployment will increase possibly to 9 per cent.
In spite of the remarks of the minister concerning the housing boom and the number of starts, in fact housing starts as of November 10 in the Atlantic area showed a Gtcime, for the first nine months of this year, of 39 per

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Carter
cent. The minister, with his usual contempt lor the unemployed ol this country, announced an immediate increase of 10 per cent in the rate of benefit for those receiving unemployment insurance. I am sure the people on the rolls of the unemployed must think this is a magnanimous effort on the part of the Minister of Finance and the government! It amounts to an additional $4 or $5 a week.
We on this side of the House feel that the government has an obligation to do everything possible to alleviate the suffering of those unemployed this winter, particularly in view of the fact that their plight is due in no small measure to the actions taken by this government in the past year and a half. If this government had any real feeling for the unemployed people it would have proposed an emergency amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for substantially increased benefits from January 1 to July 1, which will be the critical months ahead for people on the rolls of the unemployed. The increased benefits should be in line with the recommendations of the Gill report. The present ceiling on unemployment insurance benefits is $53 per week. We believe in updating the Gill report recommendations which would increase the ceiling for a man with dependants to $60.24. This figure is arrived at by calculating the benefits as 60 per cent of income. There is currently a surplus in the unemployment insurance fund of $464 million, which we believe is adequate to finance such a temporary measure.
We believe that the government should have removed the 3 per cent surcharge on personal income and corporate taxes. It is estimated that such a move on the part of the government would inject an additional $150 million into the private sector of the economy. If this government had been seriously interested in helping Canadians and in trying to stimulate the economy, not only would it have removed the surtax but it would have announced a 10 per cent reduction in personal income tax for those earning less than $6,000 per year. This would have injected an additional $140 million into the economy. This additional money would have been injected mainly into the economy of the more depressed regions of Canada where the distribution of personal income is less, particularly the Atlantic provinces.
The government's proposed amendment to the Regional Development Incentives Act, which will have the effect of including a part of Ontario and Quebec including Montreal, will be seriously detrimental to the Atlantic area, especially to the province which I represent. What chance do the Atlantic provinces have to compete with new industry when so much of the industrial heartland has been made eligible for incentives? With close to 65 per cent of Canada designated as special areas in the economy, economically depressed, underindustrialized areas can no longer have special status. As somebody said the other day-I believe it was in the Globe and Mail when everything is designated, nothing is designated. With regard to the province of Newfoundland, the only benefit we will derive from the budget presented by the Minister of Finance is the $5 million allocated to the guaranteed
loans program. Maybe we can look forward to another $1 million in Newfoundland through accelerated public works programs, but this will not achieve the objective of substantially reducing unemployment in my province this coming year.
While I am talking about unemployment I should like to refer to a question I posed to the Minister of Economic Regional Expansion (Mr. Marchand) this afternoon concerning the plight of the people in the Argentia area of my riding, where things are pretty tough as a result of the phase-down of the United States naval station three. On July 6 of this year the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) went to Newfoundland and with his usual described as an emergency assistance program aimed at flurry announced that a $2 million plan, which he softening the effects of the phasedown of the U.S. naval station at Argentia, would be put into effect. In his usual style he went to great lengths to describe them as crisis projects. They include the construction of a community stage and other facilities for the fishermen. They include the construction of a boatbuilding and boatrepair facility. They also include $100,000 in the way of boatbuilding subsidies.
The minister indicated the government would make $450,000 available by way of grant to enable the department concerned to make an immediate start on the Castle Hill national historic park. He referred to a sizeable amount of money for the reconstruction and paving of approximately nine miles of road in the area. He referred also to a recreational area in Jersey Side leading to a nature trail at a site close to the Castle Hill project. As I have said, the minister's statement did not amount to very much and the people in the area have concluded that it is nothing more than a blast of hot air. I might add that only one or two of the projects announced by the minister, on which he claimed some $2 million would be spent, have been started. Less than $500,000 of that amount has been spent on the projects and this has not provided many jobs.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
It seems the government has recognized the real extent of the emergency in words only, because of all the projects announced only two have actually commenced. If that is the best the government when it has been recognized by all concerned that a real emergency exists and a large number of people have been thrown out of work because of circumstances over which they have no control-such as the phasing down of the U.S. naval station-I would hate to see this government endeavour to bring in benefits in an area where an emergency does not exist.
In all fairness to the Minister of Transport I should say it is quite possible he is not solely responsible for what is happening in that area. It is possible he is not receiving full co-operation from the Newfoundland government. It is possible he is not receiving the required co-operation from other government agencies which are involved, and it is possible the bureacracy has taken over with its usual

December 7, 1970

lack of response to the problems facing the people of this nation.
There are a number of possible excuses that could be put forward by the Minister of Transport and his colleagues in the cabinet, but I am afraid that is of little [DOT]consolation to the people of the area who face serious social and economic consequences as a result of the U.S. naval station being phased down. I am inclined to believe that the Minister of Transport, presumably speaking on behalf of his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, has led the people down the garden path with nothing but empty promises of grandiose plans involving multimillion dollar expenditures. The people concerned in the area do not condone such action on the part of our government. Too much time has already been lost. These people have been left up in the air for almost a year, with very little more to show than they had last year at this time.
I urge the government and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion especially to take immediate action to bring relief to the people of the area who are desperately groping for a way in which to retain their independence and keep body and soul together. I also urge the government to make representations to the United States government with a view to having the existing facilities which are not now being used by the base, and are lying dormant, turned over to the Canadian government, the Newfoundland provincial government or the private sector for possible development. I have great faith in that area of Newfoundland. I believe it has the necessary potential to get back on its feet if the government is willing to go in there and do its share in helping the various groups that are desperately groping for an answer to the very serious problems facing the people.
To return to the special incentives program announced by the Minister of Finance on Thursday last, I am convinced this will have a detrimental effect on the economy of the so-called have-not provinces, especially the Atlantic provinces of Canada, because I believe by designating parts of Ontario and parts of Quebec, including Montreal, as special areas little incentive will remain for industry to establish itself in the Atlantic region. So I do not believe we have any great reason to be jubilant or to get on our knees to the Minister of Finance when he states that other areas will be designated as special areas under the special incentives program, because this will have a detrimental effect on the Atlantic region.
I do not think we have any great reason to be jubilant over the announcement of the Minister of Finance in respect of the other incentives he says are being suggested by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion when we realize that almost 80 per cent of the money allocated for special incentives will be pumped into the new Quebec designated areas. I might ask what this leaves for Newfoundland or the other eight provinces of Canada which so desperately need added incentives for industry and new employment opportunities.
It has been said that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, in lauding the program of his department
The Budget-Mr. Carter
expects it to create a number of jobs in Canada because money is to be made available to industries under the Regional Development Incentives Act. What the minister does not say, in announcing that 500 jobs will be provided here or 500 jobs will be provided there, is that he is speaking of perhaps ten years hence, and that while the industries to which assistance is provided are projecting a total employment of 500, 1,000 or 1,500 people, it does not mean they will start employing that number of people right now in 1970 or, indeed, in 1971. Some of these industries will fail. Some will never get off the ground.
I believe the minister mentioned an industry in the riding of my colleague the hon. member for Humber-St George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). This was to be a hockey-stick factory which would employ 50 or 75 people. This figure is being used by the minister and his colleagues in an effort to boost their own stock and justify the action they are taking under the special incentives act. However, the industry to which I refer never got off the ground. It is dead before it can start. Many of the plants which we hear about, and which are expected to employ large numbers of people as a result of special grants from the department, never get started; consequently, the minister is misleading the Canadian people by endeavouring to have them think he is providing these jobs as a result of special grants and other incentives to industries in certain areas.
To sum up, I would have liked this government on Thursday night, through the Minister of Finance, to have shown its sincerity and its desire to strengthen the economy by taking a number of concrete steps and making definite proposals which I believe would have the effect of strengthening the economy. I believe the government should have removed the surtax on personal and corporate income and should have made every effort to restore business confidence and lay the groundwork for the private sector to expand the economy, because true expansion can only occur in the private sector.
I believe the government should initiate reforms in the construction industry. This could be done by reducing or eliminating the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. We have heard the minister in this House express a desire to increase the housing starts in Canada and make it possible for the Canadian earning an average salary to acquire a home of his own. There is one thing the minister could have done: he could have followed the recommendation of his predecessor by impressing upon his colleagues in the cabinet the need to eliminate or reduce the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. Such a move on the part of the government would have been an expression of its sincerity in trying to bring an end to the housing problems and in providing housing for the Canadian with an average salary.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
We believe, also, that the government should increase the amount of money for mortgages available through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We believe these moneys should be made available on a regional

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Badanai
basis. There are parts of Canada where housing is more badly needed than in other areas; therefore, we believe that in certain provinces-and I can speak for the province of Newfoundland-much more money is needed for housing than in the more wealthy provinces.
When the minister referred to his magnanimous offer of $40 million for housing, this was an insult to Canadians and especially to those who are now living in substandard conditions. I say this because $40 million is not even a drop in the bucket and certainly will not go any way toward solving the housing problem in Canada. Indeed, I can tell the minister ways in which this $40 million could be spent in parts of my riding.
Therefore, as I said at the outset, the budget speech was obviously an admission by the Minister of Finance and his colleagues that they have been wrong in their policies to fight and to curb inflation. He gambled but he has lost. He is not prepared to go all the way and admit his mistake, so he is trying to soften the blow by bringing in a few temporary measures, makeshift measures, that will have no lasting effect on the economy of our country.
I conclude my remarks by repeating what was said by the Premier of British Columbia, that the Canadian people would have been 3 per cent better off had the Minister of Finance sat in his seat and not risen to make the non-budget speech on Thursday night.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that one thing as sure as death and taxes is the certainty that a finance minister in presenting his budget is immediately denounced as inept and shortsighted, no matter whether he proposes a raise or a reduction in taxes or confirms them as they are. On Thursday, December 3, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) read the budget speech, the opposition reacted as predicted. They said, "Nothing good is in it. It didn't lower taxes. It didn't forecast a surplus. It didn't raise the security pension to $150 for everybody without a means test". According to its critics, the budget was a useless exercise.
Let us examine the proposals in this document without prejudice and see whether there is anything good in them. To an unbiased observer the budget reveals a 16 months program of spending that will pour $300 million into the battle against unemployment. It will add a further $200 million to the economy to pay for the announced increase in old age pensions and guaranteed supplements.
Unemployment insurance benefits are to be increased by 10 per cent immediately. Loans totalling $150 million will be made to provinces through a fund to finance job-creating capital projects next year. A further $23 million will be allocated to federal departments and agencies for capital improvements in areas of highest unemployment, which will also take care of the province of Newfoundland. A further $20 million will be allocated to development of roads and other local services for the new Montreal international airport.
The capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be increased by $40 million for housing projects. The industrial incentives program will be expanded to establish a new system of capital incentive grants for areas of acute unemployment and to establish a system to guaranteed loans. The group of measures includes the assistance to shipbuilding announced recently by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), which I hope will also assist the Port Arthur shipbuilding yards in northwestern Ontario. A capital cost allowance supplement will permit manufacturers and processors to value investments at 115 per cent of actual cost and enjoy higher than usual depreciation on capital projects. Business enterprises that will be affected will save an estimated $25 million in taxes in the fiscal year 1971-72.
These and other benefits contained in the speech of the Minister of Finance are designed primarily to take care of those in the low-income bracket and to boost employment, and are aimed specifically at increasing capital investment in industr;al development. I congratulate the minister for resisting the temptation to cut taxes prematurely, because had he done so he would not have been able to announce a program of jobless benefits and an increase in pensions, to say nothing of grants to Canadian shipbuilding.
The official opposition's critical assessment of the measures contained in the budget does not make sense, and they have failed to indicate any positive changes that under the circumstances could be construed as being practical. As far as members of the New Democratic Party are concerned, they can always be counted on to introduce proposals to cut taxes and, of course, to introduce programs costing impossible sums of money.
The budget was to a great extent based on the proposals contained in the white paper on social security, about which the Ottawa Journal of December 1 in its leading editorial said something to the effect that when the white paper proposals are implemented, Canada will have the most comprehensive guaranteed income plan in the world. The editorial reads in part:
That is the answer to doctrinaire socialists, or dreamy idealists, who say that the white paper does not go far enough in redistributing income.
Happily, the year 1970 was our best year in international trade. The clouds that darkened our economic horizon were relatively high unemployment and inflation, and the budget was geared to fighting these enemies. I have no doubt that the government will continue to introduce measures to control both.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
While our economy has been greatly helped by healthy exports, I should like to suggest that the re-pegging of the dollar at 2.5 cents higher than it was, thus setting the Canadian dollar at 95 cents in relation to the U.S. dollar, would have an immediate impact on earnings in the pulp and paper industry, iron ore and most of the other export industries. I mention the pulp and paper industry in particular because the constituency which I represent,

December 7, 1970

along with others in northwestern Ontario, is heavily dependent upon the export of pulp and paper as well as other forest products. The increase in the value of the Canadian dollar has posed a very serious problem for most export industries. I believe that industries affected by the present exchange situation are not likely to attract capital for investment unless the government decides to revalue the Canadian dollar at a more realistic rate than the present one.
Contrary to the belief of some of our economic nationalists who are forever deploring foreign investment in Canada, we still need investment capital, preferably Canadian of course. But Canadian capital alone is not sufficient to meet the demands of an expanding economy to reduce unemployment to the minimum. It is all very well to urge increased ownership of Canadian resources and industry whenever possible, provided we do not discriminate against the non-resident investor. We should be thankful that foreign investments have made possible the standard of living which we now enjoy.
My colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), when speaking at the recent policy convention of the Liberal party in Ottawa pointed out that the economic nationalism campaign is a campaign of the rich in areas such as Toronto and southern Ontario, where there is not any shortage of capital, and is not concerned with other parts of the country where there is shortage of capital. I even find the nationalism of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) as expressed in his speech which he delivered in Denver, Colorado, hard to take. Happily, he has since declared that he had been misunderstood.
When the government tables the policy statement on foreign ownership, I hope it will not contain some of the extreme proposals made to it in the report of the House of Commons Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. I was not a member of the committee at that time but I have had a chance to study the report since it was made public. It appears that the report was approved by the committee with undue haste. It suggested, as a guideline, 51 per cent Canadian participation in foreign companies and that an alien control agency supervise and control the activities of foreign firms in Canada.
I for one would disagree most emphatically with any such proposal, and I would have cause to worry greatly were it not for the fact that I have confidence in the good sense of the cabinet to reject any such inconsiderate recommendation. I have reason to believe that this final recommendation was made at a committee meeting when only 17 of 30 members were in attendance, and of those present only 11 voted for it, one voted against the proposal and five abstained from voting. On a matter of such grave importance I submit that the report in question should be recalled by the chairman and reintroduced into the committee for further consideration.
Canadians, unfortunately, are not inclined to gamble on risky things the way our friends south of the border do, yet some Canadians resent our neighbours' desire to control something here which they brought about with
The Budgets-Mr. Badanai
American money and initiative. We should be aware that Canada's economic potential in the field of resources still requires foreign capital to develop it.
One Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Jean-Paul Drolet, made more sense than did his minister when he stated, addressing the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy convention on the subject of foreign ownership of our natural resources, that the controversy over foreign ownership is unimportant as long as the best interests of the Canadian people are being served, and that the government must work with the mining companies, no matter what country they come from, in order to best serve the interests of Canadians. I am talking about partnership between the government and private enterprise for the benefit of the community", the deputy minister said. A number of studies have suggested that whatever the criteria, foreign-owned companies do not perform very differently from domestic-owned companies and the government should intervene only when the interest of the Canadian people is not considered first.
We are concerned with an industry that has an annual value of about $5 billion and is expected to double in the next ten years. "Foreign investment," said Mr. Drolet, "comes to Canada because foreign investment is essential to Canada's economy and its growth." Capital investment means expansion, expansion means jobs and jobs mean prosperity for all. I have never heard a man working for the Great Lakes Paper Company, Abitibi, Canada Car or Steep Rock Iron Mines complaining or wondering whether the shareholders are Canadians or Americans. What employees are concerned with is continuity of their jobs. That is what we want-jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While the budget speech did not make a direct reference to pollution, this question is taken very seriously by the government. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) has been devoting a great deal of his time to solving the problems of pollution. He is an ardent advocate of pollution control measures and has succeeded in making industry sit up and take notice. Of course, pollution control will be a costly program which will have to be extended over a period of many years. The government will have to decide what is absolutely essential and urgent and what can be deferred.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, an article which appeared under the heading "Special Report-Pollution Control" in the Newsletter issued by the Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company, Limited, in February, 1970. The report reads in part.
Water is one of our great natural resources. Without it we could not exist. Our bodies need it as much as our industries do. We drink it and are refreshed. We wash in it and are clean. We swim in it and are exhilarated. We fish in it for sport and for profit. We build homes and cottages near it for aesthetic satisfaction. We build factories near it to have transportation routes and because industrial processes require it. Clean water is life-giving, yet many of this country's water sources are polluted.

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Badanai
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Pollution has existed from time immemorial. As a problem, however, its impact has only been felt since localized population densities have produced more waste than our lakes and streams can assimilate.
Pollution comes from three major sources: from human and animal waste, from industry and from erosion carrying soil and debris into our lakes and streams.
In spite of the excellent past and present work by some municipalities and industries, many of our lakes and streams are still polluted-
Water pollution has become a national problem.
One clear trend that emerges from a look at the economics and politics of water pollution control is that the politics are fast becoming more important than the economics.
"The public hue and cry," says the Pulp and Paper Magazine of Canada, "will pressure Canadian industry into cleaning up its streams over the next decade despite the cost. The only slim hope is that industry can succeed in educating the public and government to adopt reasonable water quality standards, stringent enough to keep the water clean but not so expensive that they will force industries out of business. As one industry executive put it: "A pristine pure stream would be of small consolation to a man deprived of the means of earning his living"-
Many companies have made extensive investments in waste control systems during a period when there was little if any legislative pressure on them to do it. In many cases there was some financial return on the investment. But now that governments are stepping up their requirements and introducing stringent standards, considerable outlays will be required to meet these new conditions, and there will be little or no financial return.
Money is one of the keys to solving many problems in the pollution field. The technology is advancing and with enough money much can be done to improve our environment. However, we are still searching for means that will give the desired result that the country can afford based on economics. As federal justice minister John Turner said: "The physical solution is available. The problem that remains is an economic one, and perhaps, an administrative one. It costs money to treat water before discharging it into a stream."
In the nine-year period from 1960 to 1969 inclusive, Canadian pulp and paper mills representing 75% of the industry's total production spent more than $95-million on pollution control facilities-
In Ontario alone, it is estimated that primary treatment for all mills would cost $28 million and even this amount would not reduce suspended solids to the required OWRC regulations. In Quebec, the water board estimates mills in the province will have to spend $100 million to meet the board's recently announced requirements.
Looking at the industry as a whole, some estimates have placed the further capital cost of pollution control in excess of $250 million, with an annual operating cost of $40 million, to install primary and secondary treatment in every mill in the Canadian pulp and paper industry.
On a former occasion, Mr. Speaker, I indicated in this chamber what the pulp and paper industry is doing in its efforts to control this menace. The Great Lakes Paper Company in Thunder Bay, for example, is spending millions of dollars to curb the pollutants which infest the air over the Kaministikwia River, and they are to be congratulated on their successful beginning. Of course, the most desirable condition would be a pollution-free environment, but this ideal state is only possible in a completely sterile environment in which there is no life.
It would be most desirable to have both the housing to accommodate the increasing population and the facilities
for work and recreation in a pollution-free atmosphere. But in our growing urban and industrial community we must learn to live with change. We must also recognize that people create pollution. The fact that we cannot achieve perfection is no excuse for not doing as much as we can, but we still have to be practical and realistic. The fact that the government, in co-operation with the provinces and the United States, is deeply concerned about the problem of protection of the environment on the borders of our Great Lakes is shown by their seizing every opportunity which new technology is bringing into the control of pollution.
I am also concerned about the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, which is reported to be seeking higher tolls on the Seaway and the imposition of tolls on the Welland Canal, which would adversely affect the economy of Thunder Bay and northwestern Ontario. Cheap transportation has always been vital to Canada's success as an exporter. Owing to the vastness of the country, this factor must be kept alive if we are to export surplus wheat, iron ore and other goods and supplies economically. In reverse, the price of imports would probably soar if rates were scaled up. The shippers would just foist increased fees on the consumer in the form of higher prices for goods purchased.
Ontario manufacturers, basing their business on export, are already facing fantastic competition from countries which possess a number of advantages. The Seaway Authority is running the risk of putting Canadian industry out of competition if it raises user charges and increases export costs. The result would not help to reduce unemployment. I would therefore urge the government to reconsider any proposals for raising fees on a transportation system because the net effect of such an increase would be increased prices of food and services.
In the matter of housing, every community has its problems. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has recognized the need to boost the capital budget of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Under the capable leadership of the minister responsible for housing and urban development, these problems are being tackled with vigour and intelligent application in an effort to give every family in the land a decent home.
The budget, Mr. Speaker, reflects the goals of the government: the reduction of unemployment, the control of inflation, the promotion of social justice, and it seeks to encourage a prosperous economy.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In discussing this motion and amendment, Mr. Speaker, one wonders what the main purpose was in presenting this minibudget. Some people have been unkind enough to suggest that the purpose of the budget was to retain the 3 per cent surtax. That may have been the prime objective. The whole tenor of the budget creates the impression that the government is unsure about where it is headed. It is not sure of the means to get there and does not know what it wants to accomplish. Is the main commitment to correct

December 7, 1970

the heavy unemployment situation, or to fight inflation? The budget does not indicate which.
The budget does not set out a clear plan or program to accomplish whatever end the government has in mind. It leaves the impression that the government intends to act as an umpire in the Canadian economic arena. When those engaged in the struggle fall out of the ring, the umpire will pick them up, throw them back in and tell them to try again. I quote from the document entitled "Budget Highlights" as follows:
Most economic indicators show improving trends in the Canadian economy. Employment is rising, unemployment appears to be falling-
Employment only appears to be falling! I continue quoting:
-and we have moved out of the pause in the growth of production of goods and services.
It states that there has been a pause. Nothing has been happening. The people of Canada know that nothing has happened. It has now been put on the record. I am reminded of an old saying of many years ago, that prosperity is just around the corner. The government could have used the old stock phrase rather than inventing a new one.
Latest figures suggest that the high level of exports established early in 1970 is being well sustained.
Canada's price performance compares extremely favorably with all other major trading nations of the western world.
As stated by a previous speaker, Canada has dropped to fourth place among the western nations with regard to standard of living. There is no commitment to full employment in this document. There is nothing to assure the Canadian people that they will not lose their jobs and become non-earners. There is no commitment to fully use the resources of Canadians. Some hon. members have referred to large figures. The previous speaker talked in terms of billions of dollars. Perhaps some day we will be told how much was lost in productivity because of the number of people who were unemployed last year. I wonder what the total would be in terms of houses, roads and bridges that could have been built for Canadians to enjoy.
We hear and read many statistics, but to get the true picture we must talk to the people involved. A sign on a very good house in Saskatoon indicates that it is for sale. Why? The owner, an architect, has found it necessary to leave Saskatoon because of limited job opportunities. It was necessary for him to move somewhere else to get a job so that he could support his family. A worker in a hotel, whom I happen to know, advised me that her sister had been fired from a beauty establishment because there was not enough work to keep her busy. The owner of the establishment simply advised her that her services were no longer required. These are people, not just statistics. This is the way our economy has been functioning. Farmers are told to take their land out of production. People trying to sell clothing and other items to retail and other outlets in Saskatoon are not receiving the size of orders that they normally do. There are rental
The Budget-Mr. Gleave
signs in the wholesale district of that city. These facts indicate what is actually happening to the economy.
Canadians hoped for the presentation of an economic pattern for this country in the budget. Instead they are left with the unpleasant and uncomfortable feeling that unemployment will continue to be high this winter. There is no clear indication of what will happen next summer. High interest rates continue and investors are discouraged. This affects all sectors of the economy. It affects that part of the economy in which I have always earned my living. It affects farmers who wish to invest in machinery, a feed lot or the various other enterprises involved in a farm. The government is proposing subsidizing loans for capital growth. Were will it all end?
The previous speaker talked about the need for foreign investment. There is division in the country on this matter. He is, of course, entitled to his opinion. We have reached the point where we bribe foreign investors; they are paid to locate in certain areas of Canada. I shall give an example to show how ridiculous the situation is. In the city of Saskatoon a refinery was built from scratch by local people. It was bought by British American Oil, resold to Gulf Oil and is now being closed. Well paid people are being moved out of this city, people who were employed in that industry. They are going to Alberta, to British Columbia and to Nova Scotia. Yet this was industry which we had established in that city, an industry which paid for itself from the time there was only a little service station there. All the money necessary for its establishment was earned out of Saskatoon and out of the Prairie region it served. It will no longer be there, and we are now trying to persuade smaller industries to come in.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
In another area of Canada, $6 million is going to a foreign outfit. Do you know how things will end up, Mr. Speaker? A while ago I was organizing a rural area and a chap drove me around. I asked what he was doing and he said, "I was farming up to last spring." I asked him why he quit and he said they had sold the farm. When he was a young man he told me he had rented a half section. He said he would take me around and show me. It was one of the best half sections in the area. He was very proud of it. He took me around and showed it to me. He said, "I planted those trees. That is a nice farmstead. I kept it painted." I said, "Why aren't you still there?" and he replied, "The lady who owned it decided she would sell it to her nephew."
That is where this country is heading. We shall work the land, plant the trees, improve the buildings, make a nice farmstead, and when it is done somebody else will own the thing and tell us we are through. It is time we quit being starry-eyed and decided where we are going. Mention has been made of the large sums of money which will be made available to the province of Quebec. I am not concerned about the amount of money which will be made available to Quebec, and I am a westerner. What I am concerned about is that Canada should be an operating country, a viable country economically, and

December 7, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Gleave
that Canadians should own it. Any government which runs this country should be as concerned about one section of it as it is about another. Surely, if a government has a right to call itself a national government it must be concerned about all sectors of the economy.
What concerns me most directly, though, is what is happening in the area where I live. I am concerned about whether this budget or minibudget is helpful to the hundreds of people who live in that community. As far as I am concerned, the answer to that question is no. The government has no program which would meet the needs of this community. I do not say this in a narrow sense because I realize that agriculture and industry are interdependent. Farming is not isolated from the economy as a whole but is part of the total economy. If the whole sector does well, then farming will probably do well, and if farming does well one can be reasonably sure that industry as a whole will do well. Agriculture is an industry which multiplies the purchasing power of the money it earns; this purchasing power is spread out because farmers are unable to keep what they make; they have to spend it.
A recent task force report talks about retraining farmers and taking them off the land. It is utter nonsense to say that people must be taken off the land and trained for other jobs when the rate of unemployment is as high as it is today. What jobs? Has this government ever made a commitment to the 3 per cent unemployment level as recommended by the Economic Council? When the government makes a commitment of this kind maybe we can take some of the recommendations of the task force seriously, but until it does, I for one do not intend to take them seriously. At the present time we cannot provide sufficient jobs for those who want to move out of agriculture, let alone for those whom some economists up in the ivory tower might propose to move out as well.
In the same document, Mr. Speaker, great play is made of the $100 million stabilization fund which is to be set up for farmers. This is to be a one-year shot, if it is done even for one year. Let us accept that these people mean what they say. In future years the stabilization fund will be supported by the means of a 3 per cent deduction'- and this is not to be 3 per cent off the net but 3 per cent off the gross. It will be like a property tax. Under the plan which is proposed, the farmer will pay whether he has a loss or whether he makes a profit. It comes off the top, Mr. Speaker. It is off the gross, and it is ridiculous.
There may be some who will say, "Let us make it 1 per cent, not 3 per cent." I shall not discuss this idea of stabilization in great detail because there will be other opportunities to do so, but I say to the government, "Tell the whole story; do not come into this House with half the story. Tell the people that the farmer will be contributing off the top and that he will pay this money to stabilize his income at a level which may not even be above the poverty level."
Mr. Speaker, I do not want anyone to guarantee me poverty; I can do that for myself. I do not need a government to guarantee me poverty. When they undertake to
see that the income level will be at or above the cost of production to the average efficient farmer, then they are talking about a guaranteed income, and that is a reality. But what they have been talking about is a myth, a dream. They should listen and talk to the farmers as I did a week ago, sit in a hall and listen to 25 of them and get the feedback. Then they would know what the farmers think. At present we do not know what the government intends to do. Hon. gentlemen opposite should go to meetings and get the farmers opinion.
We shall not be sure of the size of the deduction until the minister gets up one of these days to make a full statement. I have asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board more than once to make a statement on motions. It is about time he told the House exactly what he has in mind. The people of Canada pay attention to the budget and think: More cash. There go the western farmers again, money running out of both pockets and going strong.
A similar thing occurred last year when the government talked of giving the farmers $140 million. They have not yet received this money, and probably will only receive about half that amount. Not only does the government expect the farmers to pull themselves up by their bootstraps; they expect them to hold themselves up by their bootstraps once they get there. That is about the basis of the program. To offset the cost of the program the government will discontinue the storage payments and discontinue PFAA. They will try to recoup the money they spend. That is the typical approach of this government. I have been here a couple of years now and can almost recognize the pattern.
e (9:30 p.m.)
The government said that it will increase old age pensions by taking from the rich and giving to the poor. But when you examine this more closely, you find that those at the upper level of the pension group are going to finance those at the bottom. There was no mention of the rich; they did not figure in the equation at all. When the government says it is going to stabilize farm income and incomes from cereal grains, they mean they will do it at the expense of the people concerned. They are going to use the open market system to the greatest extent possible. That is one forecast that I make.
On one side you have myth, on the other side reality. When hog prices drop to 22 cents a pound or $22 a hundred; nothing happens. There is a stabilization program on hogs; the only trouble with it is that it does not work. Through this budget the government is adopting a "now you see it, now you don't" approach. It is putting up money for loans here, money for loans there; The impression is left that the drop in farm income is going to be relieved, that unemployment will diminish with the creation of additional jobs.
I sincerely hope the grain farmers of western Canada will send a signal to this government that is loud and clear, telling the government they do not accept the proposed cereal grains program. This program will not

December 7, 1970

pull the farmers out of their difficulties. I suggest the government face that fact right now, rather than slog along with the program for four or five years and then try to clear up the problems it will leave behind.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) has presented a very gloomy picture of the Canadian scene. Fortunately, in his budget speech last Thursday night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) presented a much happier picture, one in which we have reached the peak of the unemployment problem on a seasonally adjusted basis and are moving into a period of less unemployment during 1971. I suppose the voices of doom and gloom that we hear from the far corner of the House are only to be expected since the members there tend to take this approach.
This budget that the Minister of Finance presented last week tends to be a very selective document. It tends to have specific effects on localized regions throughout the country. Not the least of these, of course, is the special attention that has been paid to the sovereign counties of Stormont, Glengarry and Prescott, in which Mr. Speaker has a special interest in that he represents them in this House of Commons. I am sure all hon. members in this chamber have special sympathy for the unemployment and economic problems in his constituency. Because of the non-partisan position that he occupies in this House with great dignity, he is unable to take the government to task publicly and get them to deal with these problems. In any event, his message seems to have got through and I believe all hon. members will rejoice in his area being one of many parts of this country which have been designated for assistance in acquiring new industries.
This policy of helping areas of special need, such as areas of high unemployment, is consistent with the selectivity approach of the government as outlined last week in the white paper on social security. The approach there was not to universality but to selectivity; to put the resources of the country where there is greatest need. So with this budget, the majority of the resources are put where there is greatest need. Much of the budget's attack is directed at the fight against unemployment during the forthcoming winter months. Its approach is not only directed to public expenditure in areas of high unemployment; it also seeks to stimulate the private sector through grants to private industries which wish to locate in areas of high unemployment. In addition, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to receive more funds for loan purposes.
I suppose some historians may look on this budget as being the Quebec crisis budget, since it was presented a few weeks after the recent events in that province. In addition, the budget places a great deal of emphasis on the stimulation of industrial activity in and around the metropolitan area of Montreal. Included in this is the designation through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion of the southwestern part of the province of
The Budget-Mr. Foster
Quebec for industrial incentive grants. Some $130 million has been allocated in this regard. A like benefit is also divided amongst the counties of Stormont, Glengarry and Prescott. Funds have been set aside for new access roads and ancillary services around the new Montreal airport at Ste. Scholastique, as well as special assistance being given to the shipbuilding and footwear industries, many of which are located in the province of Quebec.
Looking at the unemployment figures in the province of Quebec and the recent events that occurred there, I believe most Canadians will view with sympathy the special problems of that province. At the same time I think there is a feeling in some parts of Canada that the provincial and municipal authorities in Quebec and in the city of Montreal have a responsibility, not only to control the violent acts that have been committed by groups like the FLQ but to provide a level of public administration that will encourage the private sector of the economy to invest in the province. If this were the case, unemployment in the province would not be of crisis proportions and the federal government would not have to present a budget that earmarked the majority of its funds for one province and for one metropolitan area. Surely this kind of budget places some strain on national unity.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Having said this I say that many parts of the budget contain benefits which apply throughout the country, including an increase of 10 per cent in benefits under the unemployment insurance fund. Many parts of the country will have very heavy unemployment this winter, and these benefits will be especially welcome. This will act as an interim adjustment between January 1 and June 30, when the new scale of benefits will come into effect. The contribution of $54 million to the unemployment this winter will help remove the sting of being unemployed during the winter months.
I am most pleased to see the establishment of a new $150 million loan fund to stimulate activity through public works projects carried out by provinces and municipalities. At a time when we have high unemployment it is most appropriate for the federal government to put funds into the hands of the provinces and the municipalities for public works projects which will create employment. I believe much of this money in the province of Ontario should be used on sewer and water projects in the small towns and communities. Practically every small community throughout the province is being pressed by the Ontario Water Resources Commission to establish new sewage treatment plants and sanitary sewers. However, the level of provincial and federal government assistance is so low that these municipalities cannot afford to carry out the work.
In many cases the municipal tax level would be doubled, and in some cases tripled, if these new facilities were provided. Therefore, I believe the Minister of Finance should designate that in the province of Ontario these funds amounting to $17 million be earmarked to

In conclusion, I find the most encouraging part of the budget presented by the minister the fact that he feels unemployment reached a peak in the last quarter of 1970 on a seasonally adjusted basis. He anticipates that our gross national product will rise during the second half of 1971 at a rate of over 8 per cent. If such a rate of growth can be achieved while we are controlling inflation, our unemployment picture will certainly show improvement. Therefore I hope the minister's prediction, based upon information available to him, is correct.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too,
join the previous speaker in expressing the hope that the prediction made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his budget speech will be a reality and that the economy will move ahead. I certainly believe it is a pleasure for everybody here to have the opportunity in a budget speech to discuss some of the problems in Canada. I think that probably the bulk of the problems we face today can be attached to the budget or to finances in general.
Although the minister's remarks in the budget speech indicate hope for an improved economy, hope that the situation will be better in the future, I believe there is still some confusion in many of our minds concerning whether the methods he uses will really do the job. It was comforting to me to see the emotion displayed on the minister's face when he listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) concerning the beauty parlour operators in Saskatoon who were being thrown out of work. It is an indication, to my mind, that he has a heart. Sometimes when we travel across the country there would seem to be an indication that the people do not believe our Minister of Finance really has a heart.
The minister has been saying that the purse strings are being loosened, whereas in reality I believe the purse strings really were loosened in respect of the banking system early last summer, although nothing really happened. Credit was eased and any business which showed an indication that it was a good prospect had funds available to it. I suggest that the announcement now that the purse strings will be eased is merely an effort to make people have a little more hope in the future. Nothing is moving ahead. The demand for money is not there. Confidence in the economy has been shattered.
There is a projection in the budget that there will be improvements in the capital cost allowance base for the manufacturing and processing industries. This is fine. Predictions were made concerning the amount this would cost the treasury in respect of tax money, but really there will be no cost to the treasury if these industries do not have the confidence and the demand for their products which would encourage them to move ahead. I question whether or not these industries will take advantage of the improved capital cost allowance base.
Then we have the matter of unemployment. This is a difficult situation. Certainly there is a trend for all people
The Budget-Mr. Downey
to depend more on government services to provide for them from the cradle to the grave. I realize a government must recognize these trends and follow, certainly to some degree, the wishes of the people. But I say we should have more public projects and that we should redirect many of our funds presently being used for unemployment insurance and various other social measures to government work projects. In character building I believe it is far more important for the people to do a day's work for the money they receive.
Arguments have been put forward that in many areas of the country people who have families should not be moved and therefore should not be offered employment in another part of the country where jobs are available. I can hardly buy that concept because we as Members of Parliament, or a great many of us, must spend six or eight months of the year away from our families. I cannot really legitimatize the argument that many of the people who are receiving unemployment insurance are not in the work force because of the mobility factor, and that they should not leave their homes at least for some period of time when jobs are available in another area. I suggest that every able bodied man in this country should be looked at again in terms of what he can do and where he can do it. The excuse that he cannot become a truck driver or something else because he is a plumber, a carpenter or has some other vocation is not reason enough for not being employed if a job of some kind is available.

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED SPECIAL MILITIA TRAINING PROGRAM FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
NATIONAL DEFENCE-SUGGESTED SPECIAL MILITIA TRAINING PROGRAM FOR YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 26 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) whether in view of the success of the summer student militia program introduced by the government, which employed some 5,000 students, he would consider introducing a special militia training program similar to the program introduced by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1961, which oriented many young Canadians into training for civil defence and at the same time tended to overcome unemployment which had reached comparatively serious proportions.
I brought the question to the attention of the minister because I was very closely involved in this training program and found it to be invaluable in many respects. My reason for pursuing my request for this type of program tonight is that I am still convinced such a program would be invaluable due to problems in our country with which evidently we are having a difficult job to cope.

December 7, 1970
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
While I am reluctant at this time of night to bring back members on the opposite side to answer my question, I do so without apology due to the offhanded answer I received from the minister, for which he is becoming famous. He ignored the common courtesy I extended in sending him not only a copy of my question but also some background notes. Members on the opposite side of the House continually are prodding for positive suggestions which they could consider, and therefore I offer this common sense idea which I feel should be given serious consideration.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
It is very evident that the government now realize the almost fatal mistake they were making in reducing the Canadian forces strength over the past two years to what was inevitably to become a state of ineffectiveness but for the unfortunate turn of events in Quebec. And as in their lack of realization of the value of military insurance against any kind of aggression, terrorist activities in Quebec, which we would all like to believe never happened, came upon this country without warning. Now I am sure they realize the need for preparedness to ensure security not only from without but from within.
The success of the summer student militia training program emphasizes the value of military indoctrination, not particularly to create military might but to instil leadership qualities, discipline and youth development, not only for our students but, just as important, for those who are still in their developing years after leaving school. Just as this training program was of considerable value to young men in our country in assisting in civil defence in 1961 when this was the thinking of our military minds, so would such a training program be of great value in training a cross-section of our country in aiding the civil power in case of a recurrence of hostility and insurrection.
Since the summer training program was so successful in combating unemployment, so would such a program continue to create a multi-purpose effect, not only to alleviate unemployment but to give the youth of our country a sense of purpose in the growth and progress of the country which they will one day be called upon to lead. While time does not permit me to elaborate further on the many other advantages, although the Minister of National Defence repeated that he was not considering such a program, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) just a few hours ago, when speaking in the budget debate, mentioned many other advantages of the training of our youth in contributing to the development of the Arctic, in supplementing the police force, combating pollution, and other ideas which are worthy of consideration.
A special all-year militia or reserve force training program should be introduced as soon as possible, under the responsibility of the reserve forces of Canada, to stand ready as a part-time force which, instead of being given more responsibility by lip service and being continually withdrawn should in fact be a supplement or back-up of
our regular forces. It would be interesting to know just how many more troops would have been available for other tasks, if the need arose, while we faced the terrorist situation in Quebec. I hope that someone with a little military knowledge is aware of the need for future preparedness.
The youth of this country are our most valuable asset; not the minerals, not the oil, not the gas, but our youth. They are being neglected because we have failed them somewhere along the line. If we keep telling them to participate and involve them only in dialogue, we are being dishonest in not giving them a sense of participation and involvement. A Canada-wide youth development or training program, or whatever we want to call it, will give them a sense of purpose and will show that we care. I urge the Minister of National Defence to consider, with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang), initiating such a program as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, last week I had occasion to ask the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) what steps he had taken or may have contemplated taking with regard to curtailing the restrictive practices of certain professional societies. Mr. Speaker, you and member of this House who belong to professional societies will know and understand that statutes in our provinces give to professional bodies a unique position in that these societies can pretty well legislate as to all circumstances surrounding the practice of their particular profession within a province.
As a result, professional societies may to a great extent regulate the fees which members charge and they may also regulate the number of people who enter the profession. I am not so much concerned with the fees charged by members of professional societies as I am with the practice of those societies in restricting the membership of a profession within a province.
My attention has been drawn to the practices of dental societies and I wish to zero in on them particularly.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion PUBLIC SERVICE-SHARING OF DECISIONS AFFECTING JOB

Mr. Speaker, no doubt many members of the federal civil service rejoiced at the statement on November 27 by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) who announced to the House in response to my question: "The government is now reviewing the Public Service Staff Relations Act." One does not need to be a specialist in labour relations to say that the period between 1964 and the present time has been one of uncertainty and instability for many career people within the service. To charge that the situation has been chaotic is perhaps overstating the case, Mr. Speaker. None the less, the reclassifications in the professional category were to have been completed by July 1, 1967 some three years ago. They have been postponed time and again, and today there are nearly 5,000 professional people, or 17 out of 28 groups, yet to be completed. These groups have to be satisfied with a classification heading termed as a "provisional assignment".
Why has there been so much foot-dragging in this? Why have certain groups such as engineers, who challenged their classification, never been given a reason for a review board ruling? Why are there the closed files? Why are most of the professional institute people "flying blindly" when bargaining for individuals or for particular services? I should also like to ask, what is the "gimmick" behind the whole classification jungle?
Mr. Speaker, my interest in this classification matter came about because it was my custom to visit inmates of federal correctional institutes from time to time. I find that when I make these visits most of my time is spent with correction staff who buttonhole me and complain bitterly, rightly so, about classification problems. Many civil servants believe that so long as the determination of classifications and duty assignment remains inflexibly enshrined as a non-negotiable right of management, in this case the government, the whole progressive system of collective bargaining is a meaningless ritual and a farce.
Suspicions abound that as the government, through negotiation, upgrades the salary for a particular classification, there often shortly follows a change in the job description and the position is downgraded. Civil servants feel that the government has it both ways. It can and does raise a civil servant's pay and, through manipulation of the classifications, lower it at the same time. The offending part of the Public Service Staff Relations Act which permits the government to do this is section 7. It provides as follows:
Nothing in this act shall be construed to affect the right or authority of the employer to determine the organization of the public service and to assign duties to and classify positions therein.
In the time remaining to me I wish to cite a few examples which give rise to the suspicion and bitterness which characterizes many public servants as a result of section 7. First, a CR-3 challenged his classification. The
[Mr. Mahoney.J
board of review reclassified the employee to CR-5 and awarded retroactive pay to March, 1968. He has received no retroactive pay to date. Why? Because the management is now reviewing his duties.
Second, under the general service classification cooks are classified FOS-6 everywhere except in Archambault, a new federal institution, where they are classified FOS-5, a saving of $1,800 per year. Incidentally, last Thursday the cooks signed a two-year agreement. However, I understand that all general services are to be reclassified as of October, 1970. Third, a technical inspector 6 was assigned extra duties. He was reclassified in the engineering scientific support group which carries the same maximum salary as TI-6. I suspect that this move was taken because a promotion to TI-7 would cost the government an additional $1,100 per year.
I anticipate that the government will take refuge from these charges by saying that these anomalies only happen during reorganization or with new positions. However, that is far from the whole story. The solutions to problems such as I have outlined lie in the government giving up some of its high-handed management prerogatives and beginning to share these decisions with those affected. I hope that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) will amend section 7 so that classification and job descriptions can become a negotiable part of the future bargaining process. It is only enlightened and sensible that this be done. The government, which is one of the largest, if not the largest employer in Canada should provide a model for other employers to emulate. It is appropriate that the Public Service Staff Relations Act be amended. The vehicle for review could be a parliamentary committee equipped to study the matter, where all the facts could be aired.
